name: Sam Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy phone accessories for Voltline Distribution, a small outfit on the business park that supplies independent phone shops and corner stores. Chargers, cables, cases, screen protectors, thousands of tiny boxes. Most of my suppliers are factories overseas, so mornings are messages that came in overnight, and I use an AI tool every day to translate them and compare quotes side by side. The fun part is spotting which cable will be the next big seller. The draining part is a whole container stuck at a port for three weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use AI every day. How did that start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I just started poking at it two years ago, on my own. Now I've got a little setup that pulls supplier price lists into one table and flags anything that jumped more than five percent. My manager, Carol, thinks it's magic and still doesn't pay me any more for it. I'm on the low end for buyers, I share a house with two flatmates, and I've got maybe two weeks of money saved after my student loan comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the tools are useful but they're not wizards. At work I'd keep showing people the little tricks that save them an hour. Online I'd probably post something like, the hype crashed but the boring useful bits stayed, and nobody got a pay rise from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd mean my edge stays small. Being the AI guy is worth a pat on the back, not a promotion, if AI stays a handy tool. And the low pay doesn't change. Two weeks of savings and a student loan is my real problem, plateau or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my little tools, and I'd try selling the same price-tracking setup to a couple of the phone shops we supply, maybe fifty a month each. I'd ask Carol for a proper rise based on the hours my setup saves. And I'd put anything extra straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit deflated, honestly, but steady. I like the tools more than I need them to change the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Carol when you ask for that rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show her a sheet: my price checker saves the team about six hours a week, and it caught a supplier overcharging us last spring. I'd ask for the money that's worth, not a thank you card. She'd probably say the budget's frozen. Then at least I'd know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned selling your setup to shops. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Ahmed, who runs a phone shop on the high street, already asked me how I spot price jumps. Small shops can't afford proper software. I wouldn't get rich, but an extra hundred a month would double my savings speed.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful but not wizards**.
I'd post that the hype crashed but the useful bits stayed, with **no pay rise** for anyone.
think: Being the **AI guy** is worth a pat on the back, not a promotion.
Two weeks of **savings** and a student loan are my real problem either way.
do: Sell his **price-tracking setup** to local phone shops for about fifty a month.
Keep building **AI tools** and ask for a **rise** based on hours saved.
feel: A bit **deflated** but steady, since he likes the tools for their own sake.
S0.quote: Being the AI guy is worth a pat on the back, not a promotion, if AI stays a handy tool.
fieldNote: His **skill** with AI is real but earns him nothing, which is what stings.
The plateau leaves his **thin money** exactly as tight as before.
He thinks in **side income** first, using a shop owner who already asked for help.

steps.text: Sell the price-tracking setup to two phone shops
Keep building small AI tools that save the team time
Put any extra money straight into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to decide who gets the gains. Publicly I'd be pro-tool, anti-layoff: use it to cut boring work, not people. Online I'd push the idea that if a firm automates buying, staff should get shorter hours at the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm better placed than most, but not safe. Buying is on that list, and Voltline only has three buyers. If they need one person to run an AI system, I want it to be me, but they might just buy software and keep none of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the ordering agent myself before someone sells Carol one, so I'm the person who runs it. I'd document everything so it's clearly my work. I'd also start a staff group with the warehouse team about how changes get made, even just a monthly meeting. And I'd keep the side work with the phone shops going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous at the same time, which is a weird mix to sleep on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be building the thing that could replace your colleagues. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest. Lucy and Marco, the other two buyers, are friends. I'd rather build the ordering agent and argue for keeping my friends as checkers than let a vendor sell it and nobody argue. Saying that out loud, I know it sounds like a story I tell myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Carol bought the software anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask to be the person who sets it up and watches it. If she said no, I'd start looking for jobs helping small firms set up these tools, probably remote, because there's nothing like that round here.

say: I'd be **pro-tool, anti-layoff**: cut boring work, not people.
I'd push for **shorter hours** at the same pay when firms automate buying.
think: I'm better placed than most but **not safe**, with only three buyers at the firm.
The firm might buy **software** and keep none of us.
do: Build the **ordering agent** himself so he's the one who runs it.
Start a monthly **staff group** with the warehouse team.
Keep the **side work** with phone shops going.
feel: **Excited and nervous** at once, a weird mix to sleep on.
S1.quote: I'd rather build the ordering agent and argue for keeping my friends as checkers than let a vendor sell it and nobody argue.
fieldNote: He'd **automate** his own team's work and feels uneasy about it.
He admits his reasoning may be a **story** he tells himself.
His fallback is **remote** AI setup work, because nothing local exists.

steps.text: Build an AI ordering agent before the firm buys one
Start a monthly staff meeting with the warehouse team
Keep setting up price tools for local phone shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public plan: an income floor and a share of the gains for everyone. I'd be loud about it online, probably louder than I should be at work. At Voltline I'd say, let's work out together who stays and on what terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my buying job and my clever setup both become worthless fast. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, it doesn't need me to run it. The warehouse staff get three more years before robots, and I'd actually envy them. Two weeks of savings won't stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on running the AI at Voltline for as long as they'll let me, and sell the setup to every shop I can while it's still worth something. I'd do a phone repair course on weekends, because fixing screens is hands-on and buys a few years. And I'd join whatever campaign is pushing for an income floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit stupid for thinking being early would save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd envy the warehouse staff. Can you say more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They lift and pack, and robots that can do that well arrive three years after the AI. I sit at a screen, so I'm first. It's backwards from what everyone told me at school. A degree was supposed to be the safe bet, and now the warehouse staff who lift and pack get three more years than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, I suppose, which I hate. They're in a small town two hours away and they'd have me back in my old room. I'd only go if I'd lost the job and the side work both. Before that, I'd sell anything I own of value, like my good laptop.

say: I'd call for an **income floor** and a share of the gains for everyone.
I'd ask the firm to work out **together** who stays and on what terms.
think: My buying job and my **clever setup** both lose their value by 2028.
The warehouse staff get **three more years** before robots, and I'd envy them.
do: Run the firm's **AI system** for as long as they'll let him.
Take a weekend **phone repair** course for hands-on work.
Join a **campaign** for an income floor.
feel: **Scared**, and stupid for thinking being early would save him.
S2.quote: A degree was supposed to be the safe bet, and now the warehouse staff who lift and pack get three more years than me.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** reversing the old idea that desk jobs are safer.
His tech edge buys him **months**, not years, and he knows it.
Moving back to his **parents** is the last resort he dreads.

steps.text: Offer to run Voltline's AI ordering system until it's fully automated
Take a weekend phone screen repair course
Join a campaign for a guaranteed income floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get the rules right if people start now. I'd post about income support and training, and I'd ask our local candidates where they stand. At work I'd suggest we plan the change together instead of waiting for a memo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to turn the AI skills into a career, not just a party trick. I'd be thirty-two in 2031. That's a few good years setting up systems for small firms before AGI makes that work vanish too. Then I'd need another plan, and I'm not sure what it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a proper online certificate in data and automation, evenings, about four hundred in fees. I'd grow the shop setup business to ten customers. And I'd start applying for remote roles helping wholesalers bring in AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but energised. Five years feels like a race I could run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure what comes after. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. I'm good at being early, but early to what? If AGI can do any thinking work, my whole plan is a staircase that ends in a wall. I'd still climb it, because the alternative is standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out of the side income, a bit each month. I wouldn't touch the two weeks of savings. Maybe skip the festival with my flatmates next summer, which would hurt more than it sounds.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **get the rules right** if people start now.
I'd ask **local candidates** where they stand on income support.
think: Five years lets me turn AI skills into a **career**, not a party trick.
After 2031 I'd need **another plan**, and I don't know what.
do: Take an online **data and automation** certificate, about four hundred in fees.
Grow the shop setup business to **ten customers**.
Apply for **remote roles** helping wholesalers bring in AI.
feel: **Nervous but energised**, like a race he could run.
S3.quote: If AGI can do any thinking work, my whole plan is a staircase that ends in a wall.
fieldNote: He'd move fast but sees his plan has a **dead end** after AGI.
He funds learning from **side income**, protecting his tiny savings.
He chooses to **keep climbing** rather than stand still.

steps.text: Take an online data and automation certificate in the evenings
Grow the shop setup business to ten paying customers
Apply for remote roles helping wholesalers bring in AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's build the safety net now while it's cheap. Online I'd push for an AI dividend, something paid to everyone from the gains. At work I'd keep being the person who shows others how to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that my job probably looks safe for a good while. I'd have most of my thirties to build something, maybe a small consultancy for wholesalers. The end point still worries me, but it's far enough off that I'd plan around it rather than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Voltline for two or three years and push to make the AI setup an official part of my job, with a title and pay to match. I'd keep the shop work growing as a side business. And I'd volunteer with a local campaign on the AI dividend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a small knot I can't untie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the knot, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That even with ten years, I'm planning a career in the exact thing that ends careers. I'm fine with it most days. At three in the morning, less so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home, with your flatmates or family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first. I'd still share the house to keep costs down. I'd tell my little brother, who's sixteen, to pick something he can do with his hands as well as his head. He'd ignore me, obviously.

I'd push online for an **AI dividend** paid to everyone.
think: Ten years means my job looks **safe for a while**.
I'd spend my thirties building a **small consultancy** for wholesalers.

fieldNote: With a decade, his **adaptability** finally pays off and he relaxes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Being early with AI is my only advantage, and two years makes that advantage worthless almost overnight. What would help is an income floor, so trying something new doesn't mean missing rent. And some kind of share in the gains for people whose work trained these systems.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people what they like about their jobs. I love the moment I spot a cable that'll sell out, and I'd miss that more than the pay, which tells you how bad the pay is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I wanted to ask.

headlineQuote: I love the moment I spot a cable that'll sell out, and I'd miss that more than the pay, which tells you how bad the pay is.
portrait: Sam is a 27-year-old **phone accessories buyer** at a small distributor, sharing a house with two flatmates.
He uses **AI daily** and built his own price-tracking setup, but earns at the low end for buyers.
He has about **two weeks** of savings, so every plan runs on side income.
In every scenario he moves **first**, yet sees AGI turning his early edge into nothing.
He leans left and wants an **income floor** and a share of AI's gains for everyone.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his only advantage, being early with AI, would vanish overnight.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor**, so trying something new doesn't mean missing rent.
A **share in the gains** for workers whose work trained the systems.
